stem: What does the ServiceNow Service Portfolio Management application enable you to do?

options.text: Document and manage your IT services using a standardized, structured format
Restore service quickly after an outage
Find the root cause of recurring incidents
Detect scheduling conflicts between changes

rationale: Service Portfolio Management is about describing and governing your IT services in a consistent, structured way — improving IT business operations and meeting customer demand, rather than handling day-to-day disruptions.

distractor_notes.B: Restoring service quickly is Incident Management.
distractor_notes.C: Root cause analysis is Problem Management.
distractor_notes.D: Conflict detection is part of Change Management.

stem: A service portfolio presents a top-level view that can include which categories of services?

options.text: Services currently available
Services that may be available in the future
Services that existed in the past
Incidents opened this week
Pending change approvals

rationale: A service portfolio spans the full timeline of services — current, future (planned), and retired/past — so you can evaluate their business impact in one place. Incidents and change approvals are operational records, not portfolio contents.

distractor_notes.D: Incidents are tracked in Incident Management, not as portfolio entries.
distractor_notes.E: Change approvals belong to Change Management.

stem: Which three entities does Service Portfolio Management let you document and manage in a structured format?

options.text: Services, service offerings, and portfolios
Incidents, problems, and changes
Catalog items, workflows, and flows
CIs, relationships, and discovery schedules

rationale: SPM centers on three building blocks: services, the service offerings derived from them, and the portfolios that organize them.

distractor_notes.B: Incidents/problems/changes are the operational ITSM processes, not SPM's structural entities.
distractor_notes.C: Catalog items, workflows, and flows are fulfillment/automation constructs.
distractor_notes.D: CIs, relationships, and discovery are CMDB/Data Foundations concepts.

stem: How is a service offering related to a service in Service Portfolio Management?

options.text: A service offering derives from a service, refining the parent service to a specific business need and performance level
A service offering is unrelated to any service
A service offering is a type of incident
A service offering is a CMDB discovery source

rationale: Think parent and child: the service is the broad capability, and a service offering refines it to a particular business need and performance level (for example, gold vs. silver support tiers of the same service).

distractor_notes.B: An offering is explicitly derived from a parent service.
distractor_notes.D: Discovery sources are a CMDB concept, not service offerings.

references.title: Service offerings in Service Portfolio Management

stem: Where does a service offering get its pricing structure?

options.text: It inherits the pricing structure of its associated parent service
It is always free of charge
It is set by the CMDB identification engine
It is copied from the incident SLA

rationale: Service offerings inherit their pricing structure from the parent service — so if the parent's model is per-unit, each offering needs a price unit, with the actual unit price set on the offering record.

distractor_notes.B: Offerings can be priced; they aren't inherently free.
distractor_notes.C: The identification engine is a CMDB reconciliation component, unrelated to pricing.
distractor_notes.D: Incident SLAs don't set offering pricing.

references.title: Service Portfolio Management service offering price

stem: What do service commitments define for a service offering?

options.text: The unique availability guarantees, scope, and pricing for the offering
The CMDB class of the offering
The on-call escalation roster
The change blackout windows

rationale: A service commitment spells out what the offering promises — its availability guarantees, scope, and pricing — which is what availability results are then measured against.

distractor_notes.B: CMDB class is a Data Foundations attribute.
distractor_notes.C: On-call rosters relate to major incident handling.
distractor_notes.D: Blackout windows are a Change Management scheduling concept.

references.title: Add a commitment to a service offering

stem: What is the role of the taxonomy in Service Portfolio Management?

options.text: A framework of layers and nodes used to organize and manage services in a portfolio
A list of all open incidents
A schedule of CMDB discovery jobs
A set of change approval policies

rationale: The taxonomy is the organizing skeleton: layers form the highest containment levels and nodes branch beneath them, giving the portfolio a top-to-bottom hierarchical structure.

distractor_notes.B: Open incident lists are an Incident Management view.
distractor_notes.D: Approval policies belong to Change Management.

stem: Which framework does Service Portfolio Management reference to bring service-related data together into a single view?

options.text: The Common Service Data Model (CSDM)
The Incident priority matrix
The Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) methodology
The Change Advisory Board charter

rationale: SPM aligns to the Common Service Data Model so that service data scattered across applications relates consistently and can be viewed together — the same framework Digital Portfolio Management uses.

distractor_notes.B: The priority matrix is an Incident Management construct.
distractor_notes.D: The CAB charter governs change reviews, not service data modeling.

references.title: Applying the CSDM guidelines to Service Portfolio Management

stem: Why would you subscribe users (or companies, locations, groups, and departments) to a service offering?

options.text: So they can order the offering from the catalog
To delete the offering from the portfolio
To grant them the admin role
To convert the offering into an incident

rationale: Subscribing entities to a service offering is what makes it orderable from the catalog for them — you can subscribe individual users or whole companies, locations, groups, and departments.

distractor_notes.B: Subscribing enables ordering; it doesn't delete the offering.

references.title: Subscribe users to a service offering

stem: Nightly backups should be a capability of the Desktop Support service but explicitly not of the Disaster Recovery service. How do you express this in Service Portfolio Management?

options.text: Apply scope to each service — mark nightly backups In Scope for Desktop Support and Out of Scope for Disaster Recovery
Open an incident against Disaster Recovery
Delete the Disaster Recovery service
Raise a change request to block backups

rationale: Scope is exactly the tool for this: In Scope items define what a service provides and Out of Scope items define what it cannot, so the same capability can be In Scope for one service and Out of Scope for another.

distractor_notes.B: An incident records a disruption; it doesn't define service scope.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting the service is drastic and loses the distinction you want to record.
distractor_notes.D: A change request modifies CIs; it doesn't express service scope.

stem: Why would you log outages in Service Portfolio Management?

options.text: To adjust the availability of a business or technical service commitment
To create a new taxonomy layer
To subscribe a user to an offering
To set the offering's price unit

rationale: Logging an outage feeds the availability math — it adjusts the recorded availability of a business or technical service commitment so the results reflect real downtime.

distractor_notes.B: Taxonomy layers are created separately from outage logging.
distractor_notes.C: Subscriptions are a different action entirely.
distractor_notes.D: Price units are set on the offering record, not by logging outages.

stem: Which application does Service Portfolio Management leverage to manage Service Level Agreement (SLA) definitions and results?

options.text: Service Level Management
Discovery
Knowledge Management
Walk-up Experience

rationale: SPM doesn't reinvent SLAs — it leans on the Service Level Management application, surfacing a module to manage SLA definitions and view their results alongside service performance.

distractor_notes.B: Discovery populates the CMDB; it doesn't manage SLAs.
distractor_notes.C: Knowledge Management handles articles, not SLAs.
distractor_notes.D: Walk-up Experience manages in-person support queues.
